sources.title: Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?
sources.text: The company counts physicists, a former journalist and an associate of the pope among its guiding lights The paper fortunes of Anthropic’s seven co-founders reached a total of more than $180bn on Thursday as shares in their company started trading at a price ahead of expectations. The opening price of $111.50 (£85) per share valued the entrepreneurs’ stakes – including the chief executive, Dario Amodei, and his sister Daniela – at between $26.5bn and $27bn each. The founders have pledged to donate 80% of their shareholdings in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, which would equate to about $150bn at the current share price. Other investors generating considerable wealth from the float and the late share price surge include Madonna’s manager, Guy Oseary, whose venture capital firm, Sound Ventures, which he co-founded with Hollywood actor Ashton Kutcher, reportedly owns 0.5% as an early investor. That stake would be worth $10bn at the opening price. At the closing price of $97.17, the combined co-founders’ stakes had fallen in value to just over $160bn at around $23bn each. The Sound Ventures stake was worth about $8.75bn. Anthropic has also committed 5% of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, which will “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”. The company has said some of the proceeds could be used to address AI’s impact on the job market , though fears the technology will lead to significant job losses have yet to be realised. Anthropic’s IPO is widely expected to channel vast sums into the coffers of a powerful social movement called effective altruism, via the many millions of dollars that its 5,300 staff will have made from the flotation. EA, as it is known, crystallised on university campuses in the US and UK in the early 2010s. It encourages its members to donate a substantial portion of their income to a set of specific causes that it deems high-priority. These include things like pandemic prevention, biorisk, nuclear safety and – overwhelmingly – the risks posed by advanced AI. Anthropic’s co-founders, including Dario Amodei, are associated with EA. Amodei took a pledge to donate his income through the organisation Giving What We Can, which is associated with the movement. However, he now disavows his association and has said he does not consider himself an effective altruist. In 2023, he told The New York Times’ Hard Fork podcast he was “sympathetic to a number of the ideas” promoted by EA, but against “dividing people up into tribes”. Anthropic’s San Francisco-born chief executive was educated at Stanford and Princeton universities. He worked at the Chinese tech firm Baidu and then at Google before joining OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT and now Anthropic’s arch-rival, where he had a key position as vice-president of research. In 2020, Amodei left OpenAI, and it has been widely reported that his departure was due to conflicting views over safety. “It is incredibly unproductive to try and argue with someone else’s vision,” he said years later. AI safety remains a major concern for Amodei. He called for a slowdown in AI development in September after the resignation of an employee who cited concerns AI could wipe out humanity and triggered a wave of concern about the existential threat posed by the technology. Amodei is also blunt about the potential impact of AI on jobs, claiming that AI could eliminate half of all white-collar jobs by the end of the decade. Amodei, Dario’s sister, began her career in politics, working in Congress and on a congressional campaign, before switching to tech and taking a job at Stripe, the payment processor. She moved to OpenAI before co-founding Anthropic with her brother. She leads teams on AI model safety and alignment , making sure AI systems adhere to human aims and values. Like other Anthropic employees and co-founders, Amodei is tied to the EA movement. She is married to one of its major donors, Holden Karnofsky, who co-founded GiveWell and the major grant-giving organisation Open Philanthropy. This Brighton-born former journalist has been catapulted into the list of richest Britons with the Anthropic flotation. His paper wealth of approximately $26.6bn (£20.3bn) compares with £38bn for the London-based Hinduja brothers and puts him above the £18.2bn fortune of the Reform UK donor Christopher Harborne and Manchester United’s co-owner Jim Ratcliffe, who is worth £15.2bn. Clark leads the Anthropic Institute, a thinktank devoted to researching the social implications of advanced AI. In a lecture at Oxford University this year, Clark predicted that an AI system will work with humans to make a Nobel prize-winning discovery within 12 months, and that tradespeople will be helped by bipedal robots within two years. He added that it would be better if humans could slow the development of the technology “to give ourselves more time as a species” to deal with the implications of its powers. Anthropic’s chief science officer received a PhD in theoretical particle physics from Harvard before working as a researcher at OpenAI, then co-founding Anthropic. He is known for his work on scaling laws – the idea that AI models grow smarter and more powerful in proportion with the resources that are spent on training them. In an interview with the Guardian last year, Kaplan focused on the major AI safety concern that animates much of Anthropic’s work – the power and potential risk of AI systems that can improve themselves. Creating such systems would be “the ultimate risk,” he said. Anthropic’s chief compute officer, who is in charge of the company’s use and procurement of datacentres, was a senior engineer at OpenAI. Given his job title, he is unsurprisingly supportive of a divisive topic in US politics: whether to build more datacentres. sources.title: Anthropic is now AI’s bellwether
sources.text: For months, I’ve been on high Anthropic alert. I suspect many of you have, too. Waiting for the S-1 to drop for months, I’d often have conversations that ended with “who knows, tomorrow might be the day.” I was even mildly anxious going off to my cousin’s wedding, beset by nightmares of the S-1 coming out while I was on the dance floor. And yesterday, watching Anthropic (a company that’s only about five-years-old) close on the Nasdaq to the tune of a valuation of $1.27 trillion (or $1.76 trillion, depending on how you calculate it), it occurred to me: Finally, AI has entered its “show me the money, for real” era. “An Anthropic IPO marks a major milestone for the AI industry, but it will also fundamentally reset the bar for startups,” said Woodson Martin, CEO at low-code development platform OutSystems, via email. “Under public-market scrutiny, inference costs, capital efficiency, and unit economics will matter just as much as the technology itself. With greater visibility into frontier lab economics, investors will demand proof that smaller players have durable moats.” Anthropic will face more questions than ever: The model maker’s first day of trading was positive but mixed, as shares soared initially to a peak valuation above $2 trillion before dropping and eventually closing up about 17%. Alone, this means zilch, but the broader backdrop was uneasy: As Anthropic traded for the first time, the market bristled with volatility, ultimately with the Nasdaq down 2.25% and the Dow down 2.19% at close. Anthropic is now a first-of-its-kind public company, with a business model that simply didn’t exist at the beginning of this decade. And this company’s untested AI-era business model—which includes Claude Code usage, subscriptions, and enterprise deals—is now a matter of public record and is financially susceptible to public sentiment. A risk, certainly, given Anthropic’s prominence in the “AI could kill us all” narrative. That accountability is by-design, said Ravi Mhatre, cofounder and managing director at Lightspeed, which has backed Anthropic since 2023 and led the company’s Series E with the firm’s largest-ever single check. “Anthropic going public is really about this coming-of-age,” Mhatre told me. “It marks an important milestone for artificial intelligence that it’s powerfully capable, being run in a company that adheres to public standards, and that implies something about transparency… It implies something about the ability for society to participate as stakeholders in the company.” Set to cash out over the coming months, Mhatre and Lightspeed are among Anthropic’s big-ticket VC backers (though, per PitchBook, the company has over 400 venture backers and no VC has an over 5% stake). The same’s true of Iconiq, which invested over $6 billion in Anthropic and had a roughly 2% stake in the company’s last round, a source familiar with the matter confirmed. Will Griffith, Iconiq partner and Anthropic backer, pointed out to me just how impossible Anthropic’s trajectory would have been mere years ago. “This is completely unprecedented in terms of a company… founded less than six years ago, achieving this scale and this level of impact,” said Griffith. “This is totally unique in history and something that the markets and the world have never seen before.” I always hesitate to call anything unprecedented, since very few things are truly, historically unprecedented. However, as a practical matter, Griffith is entirely correct: No company in history has ever gone from zero to a trillion-dollar public company in under six years, until now. But (especially in the AI era) just because a company is massive, that doesn’t mean it’s mature. Nevertheless, Anthropic is now AI’s official weather vane. “Anthropic is an important and critical bellwether of the AI ecosystem,” said Joe Fath, partner at VC firm Eclipse, via email. “There’s outsized importance that it trades well in the public markets to support the ‘AI trade.’” From here, AI will be iterating on its economics in the bright, unforgiving light of the public markets. To my mind, it’s about time. Allie Garfinkle X: @agarfinks Email: alexandra.garfinkle@fortune.com Submit a deal for the Term Sheet newsletter here . sources.title: Anthropic is now a public company worth more than $1 trillion
sources.text: The company was briefly valued at more than $2 trillion. Anthropic was briefly valued at more than $2 trillion earlier today after the company's stock began trading as part of the largest initial public offering in Wall Street history. As of the writing of this story, the company's stock is currently trading around the $95 mark. The stock debuted at $111.5 or 34 percent higher than the IPO price of $83. The company is currently valued around $1.23 trillion. Whatever way you slice it, today's IPO marks a promising start for the world's first publicly traded frontier AI lab, especially when you consider the anxiety investors were feeling about the broader AI ecosystem leading into Thursday morning. NVIDIA's stock has continued to fall following the resignation of Jensen Huang , even after the company shared on Tuesday that it had more doubled its Q3 revenue to the tune of $115.8 billion. As of Wednesday, per Reuters the stock was down 36 percent from its record-high close on October 6. Tech stocks more broadly are down following Democrats' decisive win in the US midterm elections earlier this month, as investors worry of more stringent federal regulation of AI and data centers come January. Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei appeared to attempt to address those concerns when she spoke ahead of the opening bell. "To anyone watching who is uneasy about AI or unsure what it will mean for you. This technology needs you," she said. "Not your trust, not your use, but your voice." Of course, the question now is, can the company sustain its momentum? With OpenAI reportedly eyeing a 2027 debut for its own IPO, and a resurgent Google once again competing at the frontier, the market for AI models is as crowded and competitive as ever.

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Anthropic’s Record-Breaking IPO Highlights the AI Giant’s Worst Enemy—Itself
sources.text: After closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet. But the AI lab has also committed to paying vendors more than $900 billion over the next 19 years, mostly to develop data centers powering Claude and its other AI models. Some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the company’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before. Anthropic shares, trading under the ticker symbol ANT, jumped more than 30 percent when they debuted on Nasdaq midday Thursday. The case for pessimism over the long term rests on issues that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing new tools. This month, US voters largely rejected data centers when given the chance, and protests against new projects show no signs of slowing. Delays in the launch or expansion of new facilities could leave Anthropic struggling to train more powerful AI models. “The jury’s still out on whether artificial intelligence is going to benefit everyone, or just a few people,” says Elaine Matheny, one of 70 members of Mason County United, a grassroots organization fighting an under-construction data center intended for Anthropic in West Virginia. “Do we really need to cover up all our farmland so Claude can do all our thinking for us?” Then there are the concerns about the safety and security of Anthropic’s models. At a livestreamed investor meeting last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said developing safeguards was the limiting factor in deploying its AI models. “We don’t want these agents to run wild,” he said. It’s possible the company could prioritize safety to a point that stunts growth. The San Francisco-based developer is organized as a public benefit corporation, a legal designation that allows it to prioritize societal impacts alongside shareholder interests. Amodei has said the company held back a new model earlier this year, jeopardizing sales to protect the public from potentially harmful technology. He also has said the company tries to screen for hires “oriented toward the public benefit” to ingrain the safety culture among its 5,300 employees, which is “painful in the short run” as the company passes over otherwise qualified candidates. Anthropic’s market debut is the largest for a so-called PBC, and the first for a company solely focused on generative AI development. It also represents a triumph for the handful of renegade engineers and business leaders who started it. They siphoned themselves off from OpenAI in the midst of the pandemic nearly six years ago over strategic differences, and the two companies have been rivals ever since . For some time, OpenAI was expected to go public first, but executive departures , shifting priorities , and legal troubles have introduced roadblocks. Anthropic also has some compelling numbers to show investors. Revenue is soaring , while operating losses are declining . Its big spat with the US Department of Defense this year over limits on Claude use doesn’t appear to have significantly slowed growth. Overall, the number of customers spending six figures annually is up 12 times compared to a year ago. “I don’t think you could have dreamt of an [IPO prospectus] that’s as good,” says Tomasz Tunguz, general partner at the investment firm Theory Ventures. Because of how Anthropic must account for compensating employees with stock, it’s still wildly unprofitable—over $104 billion in losses this year through September. That’s no matter when investors are eager to buy shares and lend money. The IPO raised about $81 billion (more than $107 billion when adding in private sales of shares), which is more than the $75 billion SpaceX received in June in a previous world record. Anthropic’s initial valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion fell short of SpaceX’s nearly $1.8 trillion, though the Elon Musk-led rocket maker does have a more sprawling business beyond AI. (OpenAI has been valued at $1.25 trillion in an ongoing fundraising campaign.) Anthropic reportedly sought, but failed, to achieve a higher valuation, suggesting some anxiety on Wall Street. US midterm election results have increased the possibility of new regulations on emerging technologies. Fears about the debt enabling AI data center development are rising, and a potential pullback in investment from Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden exit are deepening those worries . Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have insisted investors are bullish in the long term because demand for AI models is surging. But it’s questionable whether the companies can sustain their business without coming up with ever more powerful models that drive their profits by enabling customers to automate new types of work. Without eye-catching capabilities, customers could shift to cheaper alternatives. Some Anthropic employees have taken the safety concerns to extremes. Researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic in September, citing a belief that humanity could be destroyed within a couple of years without even more focus on keeping models under human control. But, more recently, Coxon was quoted by the Stanford Daily as saying that he might return to Anthropic because he suspects he could have “more of an impact” working on safety there. Notably, Amodei mentioned safety as a challenge even above access to electricity for data centers, which many other AI companies list as their top issue. On the ground, people opposing data centers have griped about not just higher power bills, but also construction-induced traffic and housing woes, environmental pollution, and a lack of significant financial benefit. At data center developer Nscale’s site for Anthropic in West Virginia, extreme rain combined with grading (leveling or sloping ground for construction) coincided with flooding in neighbor’s backyards. “We’re frustrated, we’re angry,” the community spokesperson Matheny says.

sources.title: Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO
sources.text: Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO. At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for. Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy. However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.” With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting. $104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry. Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest. Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day. 28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%. The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab says. More than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater. Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet. All told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run. sources.title: Google anuncia Gemini 4 Neon
sources.text: O Google anunciou uma versão intermediária do Gemini, o 4 Neon . O modelo, de acordo com a big tech, promete entregar alta capacidade de raciocínio, com velocidade e menor custo para atividades de rotina no trabalho. Ele pode ser usado de forma escalável, permitindo que diferentes áreas ajustem o nível de inteligência e o consumo de tokens. É apto para análise e cruzamento de dados, mesmo em grandes volumes e diferentes formatos, como textos, planilhas e PDFs, entre outros. Além disso, pode ser utilizado na criação e na revisão de programas de computador. Na nota de divulgação, a empresa destacou que a nova IA conquistou pontuação 61 no Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, ocupando a terceira posição do ranking geral. O Gemini 4 Neon apresentou desempenho superior ao 4 Carbon, versão mais avançada dos modelos Gemini, sendo três vezes mais veloz e custando 60% do valor de seu antecessor. O modelo começa a ser disponibilizado nesta quinta-feira, 19. Desenvolvedores e empresas podem acessá-lo pela API do Gemini. Assinantes dos planos pagos Google AI Pro e Ultra também têm acesso via Gemini ou Google Antigravity. sources.title: Google adds computer use capabilities to Gemini’s Mac app
sources.text: Google LLC today released a new version of Gemini’s Mac client that can interact with other apps on the user’s computer. The feature is available in the U.S. on launch. It requires a Google AI subscription, which equips consumer Google accounts with a broader lineup of artificial intelligence tools. The offering also includes additional storage space and certain other features. Users can instruct Gemini to launch a local app by including the command “@Computer use” in their prompts. For example, a designer could upload a sketch of a vehicle and ask the AI assistant to turn it into a three-dimensional animation. Gemini finds the local app that is needed for the task, creates a project plan and carries out the work step by step. The assistant supports tasks that comprise dozens of actions. Furthermore, consumers can use the output of a newly completed Gemini workflow to launch follow-up projects. A user could have the assistant generate a visual asset in a design tool and then turn it into a mini-app with Visual Studio Code. Gemini can interact with not only local apps but also web services. That means it can load data from webpages into programs that run on the user’s machine, as well as move data in the opposite direction and between cloud services. The AI carries out its work in a background window. As a result, users don’t have to pause their work while the assistant is running. They can track Gemini workflows via a preview pane built into the Mac client’s chat window. Additionally, Google has included controls that make it possible to give Gemini feedback mid-task. “Privacy and safety are built in: you choose which apps Gemini can access, watch every step live, pause at any time, and approve key actions before they happen,” Michael Friedman, Google’s group product manager for the Gemini app, wrote in a blog post . The Mac version of Muse, Meta Platforms Inc.’s recently launched AI agent, can also interact with local apps and data. Furthermore, a cloud-based virtual machine enables it to perform tasks even when the user’s computer is offline. Dots, a competing service from OpenAI Group PBC, offers a similar capability. Google may seek to match its rivals’ cloud-based workflow hosting features in the future. The company can also extend Gemini in other ways. Notably, it could bring Gemini’s computer use mode to additional operating systems and add features for business users. sources.title: Google boosts Gemini's ability to do 'repetitive tasks' on its Mac app
sources.text: The feature can list multiple items on e-commerce platforms for you, among other things. Google's Gemini app for Mac now has the ability to do repetitive tasks on its own. The feature has been available to PC users for a while, but now the Mac app can also access Gemini's "Computer Use" capability. That means it can now see what's on your screen via screenshots, as well as click, type, scroll and navigate programs and websites for you. You can use the capability to automate tasks that would usually take several steps across programs and devices, as long as you tell Gemini what to do in natural language. The AI app will work on your tasks in a background window and will just give you a live preview in your chat. It will not be taking control of your screen or your cursor, so you can use your Mac computer like you always do. Of course, Gemini will only be able to use the apps and programs you've given it access to, and it will ask for your approval for key actions. In Google's announcement, it gave several examples for how you can use the new capability. You can use it to list items for sale on platforms like eBay in batches. If you're selling a whole bunch of clothes, for instance, you can ask Gemini to go through the photos you took of them stored in a local folder, research their pricing, log their details and then stage their listings. You can use it to quickly fill out local PDFs, such as shipping declaration forms. You can also use it to speed up creative work, such as getting Gemini to automatically turn a pencil sketch into a 3D model.
